analysis.one_liner: Requires electric utilities to connect and credit community solar projects that renters and others can subscribe to.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend a 1978 utility law to require every electric utility to offer interconnection and 'net billing' service for community solar facilities — small solar projects (2 megawatts or less) that split their output among multiple customers. It would require state regulators and nonregulated utilities to hold proceedings and set billing rules within two years, though states that had already acted or considered the standard would be exempt. Renters, apartment dwellers, and people with shaded roofs generally cannot put solar panels on their own homes; community solar lets them buy into a shared project and get credits on their utility bill. The bill never moved past its first committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters, condo dwellers, and homeowners whose roofs or finances don't allow rooftop panels would gain access to solar energy credits on their electric bills through shared neighborhood-scale projects. Community solar developers would gain a guaranteed utility interconnection and billing pathway in every state.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters and households without solar-ready roofs

how_it_helps.text: Requires every electric utility to make interconnection and net billing service available for community solar facilities of 2 megawatts or less that allocate electricity to multiple consumers [S3].
Requires state regulators and nonregulated utilities to commence consideration of the standard within one year and complete it within two years of enactment [S3].
Exempts utilities in states that already implemented the standard, considered it in a proceeding, or whose legislature voted on it, limiting federal preemption to states that haven't acted [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Electric utilities would bear interconnection and billing administration costs, and net billing credits can shift some grid costs onto customers who don't participate in community solar. Utility shareholders would face modest competition from a solar channel they don't control.

drawbacks.text: Net billing credits offset customers' charges during a billing period; if credit rates exceed the utility's avoided cost, customers who do not subscribe to community solar can end up paying slightly more to cover fixed grid costs [S3].
The 2-megawatt size cap keeps projects small and neighborhood-scale, which limits how much total solar capacity the bill could add [S3].
The state-action exemption is broad — a state that merely held a proceeding on the standard is excused — so the bill's reach in resistant states would be limited even if it passed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to people locked out of rooftop solar is real but modest in dollars: community solar subscription credits typically trim a portion of a household's electric bill, not eliminate it. The costs are also modest — administrative burden on utilities and a small potential cost shift onto non-participants, which state regulators would set rates to manage. A reasonably balanced, low-dollar bill whose main barrier was never getting a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy Subcommittee, was never scheduled for a markup or a floor vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Jefferson Van Drew introduced the bill on August 6, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S5].
The next day it was referred to the subcommittee on Energy, where it remained; no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress [S5].
It drew only three cosponsors, all Democrats, and never received a committee vote or floor action [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Electric utilities and state utility regulators are better off: no new federal interconnection or net billing mandate was imposed, and existing state-by-state control of solar billing rules was left untouched. Households without rooftop solar options gained nothing.

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or consideration of the bill before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call positions exist; its sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats, and it died in a committee chaired by a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill would force utilities to provide interconnection and net billing for community solar, giving customers a way to buy solar power through channels the utility does not own, and requiring administrative and rate-setting work. By blocking it, utilities keep sole control of how customers access and pay for electricity.

The bill would create a guaranteed national interconnection and net billing pathway, expanding the market for community solar companies. Their gain would come through lower bills for subscribers, so their interest runs alongside participants'.
